title: The Market Gets a Roof

before.title: The Market Gets a Roof
before.text:
Every Saturday, people sold food in the town square.

When it rained, the market became wet and empty.

The town built a simple roof over part of the square.

Farmers could now sell vegetables in bad weather.

People also had a dry place to meet.

Some shops worried that the market would take their customers.

The town spoke with both groups.

In the end, the market opened only on two days each week.

The roof did not solve every problem, but it helped the market stay open all year.

title: Bread in Ancient Egypt

before.title: Bread in Ancient Egypt
before.text:
People in ancient Egypt ate bread every day.

They grew grain near the Nile River.

Workers turned the grain into flour. Then they mixed the flour with water.

The dough was baked in hot ovens.

Bread came in many shapes.

Some bread was simple. Other bread had honey, fruit, or seeds.

Bread was food for rich and poor people.

It was also key for workers.

People who built large holy places and other projects often received bread as part of their pay.

A simple loaf tells us a lot about daily life in ancient Egypt.

after.title: Bread in Ancient Egypt
after.text: Bread was important in ancient Egypt. Many people ate it often. Farmers grew wheat by the Nile River. Workers made flour from the wheat. They mixed the flour with water and baked bread. Some bread had fruit or seeds. People ate bread at home. Some workers received bread for their work. What people ate can tell us about daily life long ago.

reason: The Metropolitan Museum documents Egyptian bread making and bread rations. Avoid “every day” for every person and narrow the pay statement to some workers; use explanatory nonfiction for this historical overview. After vocabulary audit, replaced several redundant rare forms with shorter Level 1 clauses, retaining Nile and bread-making context.

title: A Roman Road

before.title: A Roman Road
before.text:
The Romans built many long roads.

Soldiers used them to move quickly.

People who sold things used them to carry food, cloth, and other goods.

Road builders used stone and small stones. They tried to make the road strong and dry.

Some Roman roads were very straight.

Small towns grew near key roads.

Travel was still slow by modern standards, but good roads made long trips easier.

Parts of old Roman roads can still be seen today.

They remind us that roads can change where people live, trade, and travel.

after.title: A Roman Road
after.text: The Romans built many long roads. Soldiers used them to travel. People also carried food and other goods along them. Road builders often used layers of stones. They made many roads strong and helped water run off them. Some Roman roads were very straight. The roads made travel between places easier, although journeys still took time. Parts of some old roads can be seen today.

reason: English Heritage documents varied Roman road construction under military oversight. The original overview is explanatory, not a single historical event; replace “stone and small stones” with natural beginner wording and avoid implying every road was straight.

title: Why Ice Melts

before.title: Why Ice Melts
before.text:
Ice is water in a solid form.

When ice gets warm, it begins to melt.

Heat gives energy to the water tiny parts inside the ice.

They start to move more.

At first, the ice keeps its shape.

Then the tiny parts can move past one another.

The solid ice becomes liquid water.

This is why an ice cube gets smaller in a warm room.

If the water becomes cold enough again, the process can go the other way.

The tiny parts slow down, and the water freezes into ice.

after.title: Why Ice Melts
after.text: Ice is solid water. In a warm room, an ice cube takes in heat. The tiny parts of water in the ice can move more freely. The ice melts into liquid water. This is why an ice cube gets smaller in a warm room. If the water gets cold enough, it can freeze into ice again.

reason: “The water tiny parts” is ungrammatical and the original implies a temperature rise throughout melting. Explain heat and freer motion with short Level 1 clauses while retaining the reversible state change.

title: A Shadow Moves

before.title: A Shadow Moves
before.text:
A shadow appears when an object blocks light.

Stand outside on a sunny morning.

Your shadow may be long.

Around the middle of the day, it becomes shorter.

Later, it grows long again.

Your body has not changed.

The Sun seems to move across the sky, so the light reaches you from different directions.

The shadow changes with the light.

A shadow can help us notice the Sun’s movement.

Long ago, people used this idea to make simple clocks called sun clocks.

after.title: A Shadow Moves
after.text: A shadow appears when something blocks light. Stand outside on a sunny morning. Your shadow may be long. Around the middle of the day, it may be shorter. Later, it grows long again. Your body has not changed. The Sun seems to move across the sky, so its light reaches you from different directions. Your shadow changes with the light. Long ago, people used moving shadows to tell time with sundials.

reason: NASA describes shadow motion and sundials. Use the correct common term “sundial” instead of “sun clock”; qualify noon shadows for a clear sunny setting.

title: The Dog and His Reflection

before.title: The Dog and His Reflection
before.text:
A dog had a piece of meat in his mouth.

He walked across a small bridge.

When he looked down, he saw another dog in the water.

That dog also had meat.

The first dog wanted both pieces.

He opened his mouth to bark.

His own meat fell into the water.

Then the other dog disappeared too.

The dog finally understood.

He had only seen his own reflection.

He went home with nothing.

Wanting more had made him lose what he already had.

title: The Golden Goose

before.title: The Golden Goose
before.text:
A young man helped an old stranger in the forest.

The stranger gave him a golden goose.

The young man carried the goose to a town.

A woman touched one of its feathers.

Her hand became stuck.

Another person tried to pull her away and became stuck too.

Soon a funny line of people followed the goose.

A princess saw them and laughed.

She had not laughed for a very long time.

The king was happy to hear her laugh again.

The young man’s simple kindness had started a very strange chain of events.

after.title: The Golden Goose
after.text: A young man shared his food with an old stranger. The stranger told him to look under a tree. There the young man found a golden goose. He carried it to town. A woman touched a feather and could not let go. Another person tried to pull her away and became stuck too. Soon a line of people followed the goose. A princess saw them and laughed. She had not laughed for a long time. The king was glad to hear her laugh again.

reason: The Grimm tale has a kind young man share his food, then find the goose beneath a tree. Restore this causal step instead of saying the stranger handed him the goose; retain the procession and princess’s laughter.
